title: Tunisia’s 2023 drought coincided with a 16.1% contraction in real agriculture, forestry and fishing value added in the revised INS accounts
period: 2019-2025 (drought culminating in the 2022/23 season), long-term observations 1951-2020

rootCauses.cause: Several consecutive years of below-average rainfall, ending in a very dry and hot 2022/23 season
Most production is rainfed (about 90% of arable land; irrigated wheat under 15% of wheat area), so output tracks seasonal rainfall

Observed warming raises crop water demand and heat stress during dry years. The NC4 attaches about 2.1°C both to 1978-2012 and to 1951-2010; its 0.03°C/year station-study estimate is consistent with about 1.9°C over 62 years and conflicts only with the 1978-2012 date (SRC-TG-885, SRC-TG-889).

dataGaps: No INM national rainfall series or official annual bulletin for 2016-2024 was opened; 2023 monthly and annual rainfall deficits are known only from press reports of INM bulletins, so they are not used.
No agriculture-specific employment loss figure for 2023 was found; the reported unemployment rise is economy-wide.
No measured damage figure for olives, livestock, fodder or horticulture in 2022/23 was opened; cereals are the only crop-level measure here (see FND-TG-701, FND-TG-720).
The ministry figure of TND 345 million climate losses (2014-2022) reaches us only through the CCDR citing a trade magazine; the ministry document was not found.
No source defines which years counted as drought years, so the length of the sequence is not agreed.

Peer-reviewed drought-index analyses were not opened in full: Mohamed et al. 2023 (Scientific African 21:e01766) only as an abstract (ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403); Ben Abdelmalek and Nouiri 2020 (Sci. Total Environ. 734:139311, 1973-2016) not at all. No SPI/SPEI analysis of 2020-2023 was found.

The GIEWS brief of 31 May 2019 (forecasting a bumper crop of almost 2.2 Mt) is in the archive, but its extract is not recorded in shared source SRC-TG-700. This record's 2019 comparison therefore rests on the World Bank's statement that 2023 cereal output was just over 22% of the 2019 level; coordinator follow-up: add and verify the 2019 GIEWS extract in SRC-TG-700.
author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: A run of dry years culminated in the 2022/23 season. The latest INS annual previous-year-price series reports a 16.1% contraction for agriculture, forestry and fishing in 2023. In its spring 2024 publication, the World…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
A run of dry years culminated in the 2022/23 season. The latest INS annual previous-year-price series reports a 16.1% contraction for agriculture, forestry and fishing in 2023 (SRC-TG-890). In its spring 2024 publication, the World Bank reported an 11% fall in agricultural value added (SRC-TG-883) and GDP grew only 0.4%. The World Bank estimates growth would have been 1.8% had agriculture and agro-industry grown at their 2022 rate (SRC-TG-883).

- **Water restrictions.** The government introduced irrigation restrictions from March 2023 (SRC-TG-883, SRC-TG-882). In April 2023 it began night-time cuts to household water supply and prohibited "l'utilisation de l'eau pour l'irrigation ou l'arrosage des espaces verts et d'autres zones publiques" (the use of water for irrigation or watering green spaces and other public areas) (SRC-TG-881). The scope of that prohibition for farm irrigation is not clear from the source.
- **Cereals.** The harvest collapsed to a fraction of normal, and the 2022/23 durum wheat crop was not enough to guarantee seed for the next season (SRC-TG-700).
- **Recovery.** Output recovered in 2024 (about 1.5 million t of cereals) and 2025 (about 1.7 million t, 18% above the five-year average) (SRC-TG-700).

The evidence supports "a severe multi-year drought with large agricultural losses, followed by recovery". It does not support "a continuous 2016-2024 drought" or "an observed long-term decline in rainfall".

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
The symptom is crop failure and a fall in value added. The direct cause is the climatic shock: several below-average rainfall years ending in the very dry, hot 2022/23 season (SRC-TG-883, SRC-TG-700). The cause of the large economic effect is structural exposure:

- **Rainfed dominance.** About 90% of arable land is rainfed (SRC-TG-881), and irrigated wheat is under 15% of wheat area (SRC-TG-700).
- **Irrigation buffer reduced.** In the worst year the authorities restricted irrigation, reducing the irrigated sector's buffer (SRC-TG-883).
Warming is a background aggravating factor. The 4th National Communication attaches about +2.1°C to both 1978-2012 and 1951-2010 (INM 2015) (SRC-TG-885). The abstract of a peer-reviewed 16-station study reports significant warming of about 0.03°C per year over 1958-2020 (SRC-TG-889, abstract only). Over 62 years, that rate implies about 1.9°C, consistent with the NC4's 1951-2010 dating; the discrepancy is with its 1978-2012 dating, not with the amount of warming over the longer period. The warming direction is consistent across these sources.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
**Measured damage.**

- **Risk financing and loss allocation.** These facts describe who bears the losses, not why output fell: agricultural insurance was 0.42% of premiums in 2021 (SRC-TG-881). The CCDR reports, citing the agriculture ministry through a trade magazine, that 40% of TND 345 million in climate-hazard losses over 2014-2022 was borne by the state (SRC-TG-881).

- **Value added:**
  - -9% in real terms in H1 2023 against H1 2022 (SRC-TG-882).
  - -11.2% in first-half value added between 2019 and 2023 (SRC-TG-882).
  - -11% for full-year 2023 (SRC-TG-883).

  The -11% and the -11.2% are different measures and should not be confused.
- **Cereal output.** The estimates for 2023 disagree:
  - CCDR: a forecast fall "from 750,000 to 250,000 t", barely enough for seed (SRC-TG-881).
  - World Bank: -61% against 2022 on Office des Céréales sales data, just over 22% of the 2019 level (SRC-TG-883).
  - GIEWS: 302,000 t in November 2023, revised to 520,000 t in May 2024 (SRC-TG-700).

  OdC sales measure grain collected, not the full harvest, which partly explains the spread. Detailed cereal analysis is in FND-TG-701.
- **Seed system.** Four consecutive drought years weakened the seed production system (SRC-TG-700).
- **Labour.** Unemployment rose from 15.2% (Q4 2022) to 16.4% (Q4 2023). The World Bank attributes this partly to agriculture and construction, but gives no agriculture-only figure (SRC-TG-883).

**How long was the drought? Sources disagree.**

- **Sixth year:** the World Bank's Autumn 2023 monitor calls 2023 the sixth consecutive year of below-average rainfall (SRC-TG-882).
- **Fourth year:** its Spring 2024 monitor calls it the fourth (SRC-TG-883).
- **Four years since 2019:** the CCDR speaks of four drought years since 2019 (SRC-TG-880, SRC-TG-881).

  The Spring 2024 monitor is internally inconsistent: it calls 2023 the fourth consecutive drought year and also describes dry conditions over the previous four years (SRC-TG-883). FAO GIEWS likewise describes four consecutive years in its May 2024 brief (SRC-TG-700). The Autumn 2023 monitor's sixth-year framing remains inconsistent with these later accounts (SRC-TG-882).

Cereal output in 2023 is described as just over 22% of the 2019 level (SRC-TG-883), which implies 2019 was a good harvest year. A continuous drought from 2016 is therefore not supported; the common framing of "2016-2024" should be read as "several dry spells, worst in 2020-2023". The 4th National Communication separately refers to a 2016-2018 drought (SRC-TG-885).

**Long-term observed rainfall trend.**

- **The 4th National Communication contradicts itself:**
  - It reports a slight, non-significant upward rainfall trend for 1978-2012 (SRC-TG-885, p. 19).
  - It also cites INM's 2015 finding of a 2-16% decline relative to 1961-1990, and an increase in drought-affected area and in extreme-drought frequency (SRC-TG-885, p. 130).
- **Peer-reviewed station study:** the abstract of a 16-station study for 1958-2020 reports no statistically significant annual rainfall trend at any station (SRC-TG-889, abstract only; full text not opened).

The robust observed signal is warming; an observed rainfall decline is contested. The drying is a projection (FND-TG-880), not yet an established measured trend.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Water.** The drought turned into a water-allocation crisis. Irrigation was restricted from March 2023, and from April 2023 night-time household water cuts were added to a prohibition on using water for irrigation and for watering public green spaces (SRC-TG-881, SRC-TG-883).
- **Groundwater.** The 4th National Communication reports that after the 2016-2018 drought farmers offset surface-water shortfalls with groundwater, even saline groundwater. This kept measured production losses small but transferred the stress to aquifers (SRC-TG-885); see the water lane's groundwater records.
- **Fiscal.** Cereal import requirements for 2023/24 were forecast at 4.7 million t, about 30% above the previous year's average requirement (SRC-TG-700). This adds to the import bill and the subsidy burden (see FND-TG-700, FND-TG-702).

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- The CCDR mentions budget compensation through a fund for climate-related agricultural losses ("Fonds pour les pertes agricoles liées au climat"), and for SMEs through the 2011 Fund and Law 24-2019 (SRC-TG-881, p. 11)
- Index-based or area-yield agricultural insurance (recommended in the World Bank CCDR and the Autumn 2023 Economic Monitor)
- Plan National de la Sécheresse 2020 (updated National Drought Plan), NDC adaptation measure 8 (SRC-TG-884)
- Hydrometeorological services and early warning (recommended in the CCDR and the 4th National Communication)
- Emergency seed supply for the season after a drought harvest (gap flagged by GIEWS, SRC-TG-700)

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content: INS’s 3 August 2026 national accounts give -16.1% for calendar 2023 and +8.6% for 2024 in agriculture, forestry and fishing at previous-year prices. The spring 2024 World Bank estimate (-11%) is preserved as an earlier publication, separate from half-year measures. The annual accounts do not isolate the causal share attributable to drought (SRC-TG-890, SRC-TG-883).

resolvedSources.title: GIEWS Country Brief: The Republic of Tunisia (archive of briefs 2010-2026)
resolvedSources.publisher: FAO Global Information and Early Warning System (GIEWS)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Brief of 29 November 2023 (archive PDF, brief dated 29-November-2023):

> Cereal cultivation is mostly rainfed, resulting in significant year-on-year variations. The irrigated wheat area represents less than 15 percent of the total wheat planted area.

> Coupled with above-average temperatures during the critical crop development stages, severe drought conditions, not experienced in the country for over two decades, constrained crop development, leading to widespread crop failures. Consequently, 2023 cereal output was estimated at 302 000 tonnes, almost 80 percent below the average.

> In 2023, the guaranteed farmgate prices of durum wheat increased to TDD 1 300 (USD 436), up from TDD 1 000/tonne (USD 339). The guaranteed farmgate prices of soft (common) wheat increased from TDD 800 (USD 271) to TDD 1 000/tonne (USD 336) and those of barley from TDD 690 (USD 233) to TDD 800 (USD 267). In 2023, the government purchased 225 600 tonnes of grains, compared to 700 000 tonnes in 2022.

> Cereal import requirements in the 2023/24 marketing year (July/June) are forecast at 4.7 million tonnes, about 30 percent above the average import requirements of the previous year. More than half of the imported cereals is wheat.

> Between 2016 and 2020, the country sourced almost 40 percent of its wheat imports from Ukraine, 7 percent from the Russian Federation and the rest from various European Union countries.

> In spite of the country's high import dependency rate, changes in international prices of wheat products and vegetable oil are not fully transmitted into domestic prices as the government's universal food subsidy programme keeps them stable. There have been discussions about reforming the subsidy system, which puts a significant burden on the national budget, but the implementation has been postponed so far.

Brief of 30 May 2024:

> The aggregate 2023 cereal output, mainly wheat, is estimated at 520 000 tonnes, about 70 percent below the five-year average.

> The country relies heavily on grain imports, even in years with good domestic production, and cereals constitute the largest share of the value of imports.

> Imports cover more than half of the country's cereal consumption needs. Cereal imports in the 2023/24 marketing year (July/June) are forecast at 4 million tonnes and above the five-year average.

> Durum wheat for couscous and pasta, and soft wheat for bread, represent the main components of the local diet and account for around 45 percent of the food calorie intake.

> Four consecutive years of drought have weakened the seed production system and the 2022/23 harvest of durum wheat was not sufficient to guarantee seeds for the 2023/24 campaign. As a consequence, the government increased imports of wheat seed, while some farmers decided to shift to barley production.

> In the period between July 2023 and May 2024, the Russian Federation and Ukraine supplied about half of the wheat imports to the country, while about 30 percent was supplied by Bulgaria and Turkey.

> the rise of international food prices translated into increased value of subsidies leading to public debt growth and reduced the country's import capacity, causing shortages of basic food products such as wheat, coffee, tea and vegetable oils.

Brief of 27 July 2022:

> The country aims to reach an annual domestic production of 3 million tonnes of cereals to achieve self-sufficiency.

> In 2022, the average import prices of durum wheat so far reached USD 665/tonne, up from USD 435 in 2021 and USD 327 in 2020. Likewise, import prices paid for 1 tonne of soft (common) wheat increased from USD 231 in 2020 to USD 307 in 2021 and USD 416 in 2022.

Brief of 26 March 2025:

> Cereal production in 2024 is estimated at about 1.5 million tonnes, nearly three times higher than the drought-affected 2023 output, yet remaining about 6 percent below the five-year average.

Brief of 18 February 2026:

> Cereal production in 2025 is estimated at about 1.7 million tonnes, nearly 18 percent above the five-year average, reflecting improved weather conditions during the second half of the season. Although the season started with dry weather conditions between October 2024 and February 2025, above-average rainfall amounts between April and May boosted yields in key producing regions.

> Although local production has increased over the past two years, it covers about 60 percent of domestic annual needs and the country continues to rely on international markets to secure an adequate supply of wheat for local consumption.
resolvedSources.notes: The archive PDF was downloaded and converted with pdftotext; the extracts above are prose paragraphs, not tables. GIEWS revised its 2023 estimate from 302 000 t (Nov 2023) to 520 000 t (May 2024); both values are kept. GIEWS figures are FAO estimates built on its Country Cereal Balance Sheet, not Tunisian official statistics. Marketing year is July/June.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Country Climate and Development Report: Executive Summary
resolvedSources.extracts:
Executive summary, p. ii (PDF p. 2):

> Some of these effects are already taking a toll. Four years of drought conditions culminated in a significant drop in Tunisia's agricultural production in 2022/23.

p. iv (PDF p. 4):

> By 2050, a simultaneous increase in the frequency and the intensity of climate change-induced extreme weather events is expected to drive a decline in water availability, with demand outstripping supply by 28% under a representative concentration pathway of 8.5 (RCP 8.5), which is the worst-case climate change scenario (Figure 2).

> Agricultural losses, especially in Tunisia's main agriculture systems (olive, oasis, cereal, and livestock), also increase, as do the incidence of disease, with the poor being the most vulnerable to these compounding impacts.

Footnote 2, p. iv:

> While long-term greenhouse gas emissions under an RCP 8.5 scenario are widely considered overly pessimistic, the Coupled Model Implementation Project (CMIP) climate change scenarios with RCP 8.5 (CMIP 5) provides a useful (and not implausible) high-warming forecast

p. vi (PDF p. 6):

> Our modeling suggests that, compared with a baseline based on past trends, unaddressed water shortages, coastal erosion, and flooding could reduce real GDP by 3.4 percent in 2030 (under RCP 8.5). These annual losses could grow to 6.4 percent of GDP by 2050, or TD 10.4 billion (US$3.4 billion) in net present value terms. A large share of these losses is driven by the impacts of water shortages. The agricultural sector would therefore be particularly affected, with its value added expected to fall by 15 percent by 2030 (and by 29 percent by 2050).

> A decline in agricultural production would reduce net exports, while imports would increase to bridge the resulting supply-demand gap.
resolvedSources.notes: 16-page executive summary of the CCDR, downloaded as PDF and converted with pdftotext. The 15% (2030) and 29% (2050) value-added losses come from the CCDR macro model (World Bank MFMOD combined with a Baqaee-Farhi multisector model, see SRC-TG-881, Box 10). They are driven mainly by projected water shortage under RCP 8.5 and measured against a past-trend baseline. They are model outputs, not observations. The full report (SRC-TG-881) gives the method and footnotes.

resolvedSources.title: Country Climate and Development Report: Tunisie (full report, French version)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Section 1.2, p. 4 (PDF p. 27), captions of figures 9 and 10:

> Figure 9: Dans le pire des scénarios de changement climatique, la température augmente de 2°C à 2,3°C jusqu'en 2050 et de 4,1°C à 5,2°C jusqu'en 2100

> Figure 10: Dans le pire des scénarios de changement climatique, les précipitations diminuent de 1 à 14 % jusqu'en 2050, et de 18 à 27 % jusqu'en 2100

English gloss: In the worst-case scenario (RCP 8.5, footnote 21), temperature rises 2-2.3°C by 2050 and 4.1-5.2°C by 2100; precipitation falls 1-14% by 2050 and 18-27% by 2100.

Footnote 22, p. 4:

> Les chiffres variant en fonction de la source de données et de la méthodologie utilisée. Selon un site web officiel du gouvernement (https://climat-c.tn/INM/web/precipitation), les précipitations pourraient diminuer de 6 % dans le cadre d'un scénario RCP 4.5 et de 9 % dans le cadre d'un scénario RCP 8.5 d'ici à 2050. Les températures pourraient augmenter de 1,6°C dans le cadre du scénario RCP 4.5 et de 1,9°C dans le cadre du scénario RCP 8.5 d'ici 2050

English gloss: Figures vary with data source and method. The official INM site gives -6% (RCP 4.5) and -9% (RCP 8.5) precipitation, and +1.6°C / +1.9°C, by 2050.

Section 1.2.1, p. 7 (PDF p. 30):

> Après quatre années consécutives de sécheresse depuis 2019, le stress hydrique est devenu encore plus grave. La saison des récoltes de la plupart des cultures a été gravement affectée. Par exemple, la production de céréales devrait passer de 750 000 à 250 000 tonnes métriques lors de la saison 2022/23, une quantité à peine suffisante pour la production de semences. En avril 2023, le gouvernement a commencé à mettre en oeuvre des coupures nocturnes de l'approvisionnement en eau dans les foyers et à interdire l'utilisation de l'eau pour l'irrigation ou l'arrosage des espaces verts et d'autres zones publiques.

English gloss: After four consecutive drought years since 2019, the harvest of most crops was badly affected. Cereal production was expected to fall from 750,000 to 250,000 t in 2022/23, barely enough for seed. In April 2023 the government began night-time household water cuts and banned water use for irrigation and for watering public green spaces.

p. 8 (PDF p. 31):

> Le secteur agricole est important pour l'économie nationale, contribuant à hauteur de 9,6 % du PIB en 2022 et employant 14 % de la population active en 2019

> Bien que 90 % des terres arables soient pluviales, l'agriculture irriguée consomme la plus grande partie de l'eau et contribue à 36 % de la valeur ajoutée de l'agriculture

English gloss: Agriculture was 9.6% of GDP in 2022 and employed 14% of the labour force in 2019. Although 90% of arable land is rainfed, irrigated agriculture uses most of the water and provides 36% of agricultural value added.

p. 9 (PDF p. 32):

> Dans le cadre d'un scénario d'émissions stabilisées (RCP 4.5), la fréquence des années sèches en Tunisie devrait augmenter de 52 % (10 années sur 19) entre 2031 et 2050. Cette fréquence passera à 79 % (15 années sur 19) dans le cadre du scénario RCP 8.5, ce qui aggravera la situation déjà difficile de l'eau, en particulier dans le secteur agricole et les zones rurales

English gloss: Under RCP 4.5 the frequency of dry years is projected to "increase by 52% (10 years out of 19)" in 2031-2050; under RCP 8.5 it reaches 79% (15 of 19 years), worsening the water situation especially for agriculture and rural areas.

p. 11 (PDF p. 34):

> L'assurance agricole est émergente, représentant 0,42 % du volume total des primes d'assurance en 2021

> Selon le ministère tunisien de l'Agriculture, les pertes dues aux aléas climatiques catastrophiques au cours des huit dernières années (2014 à 2022) s'élèvent à 345 millions de dinars (112 millions de dollars), dont 40 % ont été pris en charge par l'État

(footnote 62 gives the source as "Atlas Magazine, 2023".)

> Des compensations par le biais d'instruments budgétaires ont également été prévues pour les pertes directes subies par les PME (par exemple, par le biais du Fonds 2011 et de la loi 24-2019) et par le secteur agricole (par exemple, par le biais du Fonds pour les pertes agricoles liées au climat).

English gloss: Agricultural insurance is emerging, at 0.42% of total insurance premiums in 2021. Budget compensation exists for SMEs (2011 Fund, Law 24-2019) and for agriculture (a fund for climate-related agricultural losses). According to the agriculture ministry, losses from catastrophic climate hazards over 2014-2022 total TND 345 million (USD 112 million), 40% of it borne by the state.

Section 3.1.1, p. 25 (PDF p. 48):

> La production agricole devrait chuter de 29,1 % dans le cadre des scénarios RCP 4,5 et de 33,1 % dans le cadre du scénario RCP 8,5 par rapport aux projections réalisées dans le cadre d'un scénario sans stress climatique. Aux prix actuels de 2022, ces pertes se traduiraient par 4.0 et 4,6 milliards de dinars, soit entre 2,8 et 3,2 % du PIB. Ces pertes sectorielles directes (équilibre partiel) engendreraient ensuite des pertes macroéconomiques (équilibre général).

English gloss: Agricultural production would fall 29.1% (RCP 4.5) and 33.1% (RCP 8.5) relative to a no-climate-stress projection. At 2022 prices this is TND 4.0-4.6 billion, 2.8-3.2% of GDP (partial-equilibrium sector losses). The paragraph opens with water losses "d'ici à 2050" (by 2050).

p. 24 (PDF p. 47):

> La baisse prévue du rendement des olives, qui représentaient 40 % des exportations agricoles totales en 2019, pourrait atteindre 69 % sous RCP 8.5. Le blé tendre et l'orge devraient connaître des baisses similaires du rendement (baisse de 35 % pour le blé tendre et de 41 % pour l'orge) d'ici 2050 sous RCP 8.5

> Les changements climatiques devraient également entraîner la perte d'au moins 30 % des emplois agricoles d'ici 2050, en raison notamment de la désertification irréversible des oasis du pays, où l'agriculture est la principale source de revenus

Footnotes 89, 90 and 93:

> 89 Agence française de développement 2020.

> 90 Dans le cadre du RCP 4.5, les rendements pourraient diminuer de 67 % pour l'huile d'olive, de 42 % pour le blé tendre et de 54 % pour l'orge.

> 93 Ministère de l'Environnement 2021.

English gloss: Projected olive yield loss could reach 69% under RCP 8.5; soft wheat -35% and barley -41% by 2050 under RCP 8.5 (citing AFD 2020). Under RCP 4.5: olive oil -67%, soft wheat -42%, barley -54%. Climate change would also cause the loss of at least 30% of agricultural jobs by 2050, notably through irreversible desertification of oases (citing Ministry of Environment 2021).

Box 10, p. 52 (PDF p. 75):

> Le CCDR combine le modèle macroéconomique et fiscal de la Banque mondiale (MFMOD) avec un modèle d'économie ouverte multisectorielle de pointe, suivant l'approche de Baqaee et Farhi (2021)

English gloss: The CCDR combines the World Bank macro-fiscal model (MFMOD) with a multisector open-economy model following Baqaee and Farhi (2021).

Extracts added for the soil findings (FND-TG-800):

p. 8 (water and ecosystems section):

> L'envasement accumulé dans les barrages réduit leur capacité de stocker les eaux de surface ; en effet, en 2021, les grands barrages avaient accumulé un taux d'envasement moyen de 22,59 %

> La dégradation des terres a entraîné un impact économique estimé entre 2 et 7 % du PIB national chaque année

Footnote 45: "Note sur le secteur de l'eau, CCDR Tunisie, avril 2023."

English gloss: in 2021 large dams had an average accumulated siltation rate of 22.59%; land degradation has an estimated economic impact of 2-7% of national GDP per year (source: internal CCDR water-sector note, April 2023, method not given).

p. 24:

> D'ici 2050, les changements climatiques pourraient dégrader davantage les écosystèmes critiques et les sols de la Tunisie de 28 % supplémentaires en vertu du SSP3, ce qui est lié à une augmentation de l'érosion des sols (figure 19) et à une réduction des rendements en eau, de la qualité des sols et de la capacité de stockage des écosystèmes.

Figure 19 caption: "Érosion des sols dans le bassin versant de Siliana en 2020 (à gauche) et en 2050 selon le scénario SSP3 (à droite, projection)"; legend "Risques d'érosion des sols (t/ha/année)"; "Source : Générée par les experts de la Banque mondiale". Footnote 94: ecosystem services mapped and valued with the InVEST model.

English gloss: by 2050 climate change could degrade Tunisia's critical ecosystems and soils by a further 28% under SSP3, linked to increased soil erosion; the metric behind "28 %" is not defined in the main text.
resolvedSources.notes:
French translation of the full CCDR. Retrieved from a mirror hosted by the Tunisian media site inkyfada, because the World Bank Open Knowledge download returned an HTML page. The content matches the World Bank executive summary (SRC-TG-880) where they overlap. Page numbers are the printed page numbers of the report body; PDF pages in brackets.

- The yield figures on p. 24 cite "AFD 2020". The bibliography (p. 78) gives the source as: "Agence française de développement. 2020. "Impacts des effets du changement climatique sur la sécurité alimentaire." Disponible : http://www.onagri.nat.tn/uploads/Etudes/4a.%20Impacts%20des%20effets%20du%20CC%20-%20securite%20alimentaire.pdf". The source-verifier reports that this URL serves the same April 2021 deliverable as SRC-TG-886. The CCDR's soft wheat (-35%) and barley (-41%) yield losses "by 2050" under RCP 8.5 do not match that document's Table 9, which gives -13.0% and -11.2% at 2050 and -33.2% and -31.5% at 2100 (SRC-TG-886). The CCDR's olive -69% (no horizon in the sentence) is closest to the study's 2100 RCP 8.5 olive yield values: -61% in Table 10, about 66% in the text. See FND-TG-880.
- Footnote 90 gives larger losses under RCP 4.5 than under RCP 8.5, without explanation.
- "Dry year" is not defined in the p. 9 passage, and "augmenter de 52 % (10 années sur 19)" reads as a frequency of 52%, not an increase of 52%.
- The 345 MDT loss figure rests on a trade-press citation (Atlas Magazine), so treat it as tier C.
- The 30% job-loss figure cites a Ministry of Environment 2021 document that the report does not identify further.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisie Bulletin de Conjoncture Économique, Automne 2023: Migration dans un contexte économique complexe
resolvedSources.extracts:
Overview, p. 1:

> Une sixième année consécutive de précipitations inférieures à la moyenne a compromis la production agricole du pays, avec une valeur ajoutée sectorielle en baisse de 9 pour cent en termes réels au premier semestre 2023 par rapport à la même période en 2022.

English gloss: A sixth consecutive year of below-average rainfall compromised agricultural production; sector value added fell 9% in real terms in H1 2023 versus H1 2022.

p. 2:

> Le manque de précipitations au cours des 5 premiers mois de 2023 a aggravé les effets des conditions climatiques difficiles qui prévalaient en Tunisie au cours des 6 dernières années, obligeant le gouvernement à introduire des restrictions d'irrigation en mars 2023.

> les superficies cultivées en blé ont diminué régulièrement ces dernières années (de 1,5 million d'hectares en 2011 à 1,1 million en 2021). Cela s'explique principalement par la baisse de productivité due à des précipitations plus variables et à l'appauvrissement des sols, ainsi qu'à des prix de vente défavorables, fixés par l'Office tunisien des céréales (Office des Céréales -- OdC).

> Ainsi, la production céréalière nationale a chuté de presque deux tiers par rapport à l'année dernière. Cela représente un peu plus d'un quart du niveau de la même période en 2020. Cette trajectoire illustre l'évolution d'une tendance plus globale du secteur agricole, dont la valeur ajoutée au premier semestre a chuté de 11,2 pour cent entre 2019 et 2023 (figure 3).

English gloss: Lack of rain in the first five months of 2023 compounded six years of difficult conditions, forcing irrigation restrictions in March 2023. Wheat area fell from 1.5 million ha (2011) to 1.1 million ha (2021), mainly because of lower productivity from more variable rainfall and soil depletion, and unfavourable OdC prices. National cereal production fell by almost two thirds year on year, to just over a quarter of the 2020 level; first-half agricultural value added fell 11.2% between 2019 and 2023.

Box 1, p. 3:

> D'ici 2050, les ressources globales en eau par personne et par an pourraient diminuer jusqu'à 66 pour cent (de 366 m³ à 122 m³).

> La Banque mondiale prévoit que la production d'olives, qui représentaient 40 pour cent du total des exportations agricoles en 2019, pourrait diminuer par 69 pour cent d'ici 2050.

> La production agricole devrait chuter entre 29,1 et 33,1 pour cent par rapport aux projections dans un scénario sans stress climatique. Cela aura des conséquences négatives plus prononcées sur les ruraux pauvres, qui disposent de moins de ressources pour faire face aux impacts climatiques. Ces pertes se traduiraient par une réduction du PIB réel comprise entre 4,1 et 4,6 pour cent.

English gloss: The World Bank projects that olive production (40% of agricultural exports in 2019) could fall 69% by 2050. By 2050 water resources per person per year could fall up to 66% (366 to 122 m³). Agricultural production is projected to fall 29.1-33.1% relative to a no-climate-stress scenario, hitting the rural poor hardest; these losses would cut real GDP by 4.1-4.6%.
resolvedSources.notes: French edition. The "sixth consecutive year" wording contrasts with "4th consecutive year" in the Spring 2024 edition (SRC-TG-883) and "four years" in the CCDR (SRC-TG-880). Box 1 is a preview of the CCDR results and cites AFD (2020) for the water figures; it is not an independent estimate. The cereal fall is based on OdC sales data (footnote 1), not on harvest statistics.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Economic Monitor, Spring 2024: Renewed Energy to the Economy
resolvedSources.extracts:
Section 1, p. 1:

> The economy grew by 0.4 percent in real terms during 2023, with a significant deterioration since the second quarter linked to the effects of the drought (figure 1). The 4th consecutive year of below than average rainfall led the government to ration water usage since March.

> Agriculture was the main driver of the 2023 economic slowdown, as the drought exposed the deficiencies of a sector that needs to adapt to climate change. The lack of rainfall throughout 2023 aggravated the dry conditions prevailing in Tunisia over the previous 4 years, forcing the government to introduce irrigation restrictions since March.

> The dry conditions precipitated the production losses, as the bulk of cereal production is rainfed. Hence, domestic cereal production in 2023 dropped by 61 percent compared to 2022, reaching just over 22 percent of the level in 2019. As a result, in 2023 agricultural value added fell by 11 percent in real terms, aggravating the declining trend since 2019 (figure 3). Had agriculture and agro-industry grown at the (modest) rate of 2022 (1.7 percent), the economy would have expanded by 1.8 percent in 2023, slightly below the 2022 rate (2.6 percent).

Footnote 1, p. 1:

> That is based on sales data from OdC.

p. 2:

> As labor-intensive sectors (i.e., agriculture and construction) were particularly hit by the slowdown, unemployment grew to 16.4 percent in Q4 2023 up from 15.8 percent in the previous quarter and 15.2 percent a year earlier.
resolvedSources.notes: Downloaded as PDF and converted with pdftotext. The value-added figures rest on INS national accounts as processed by the World Bank; the cereal figures rest on OdC (Office des Céréales) sales data, which measure collected grain, not total harvest. The macro table at the end of the document did not convert cleanly and was not used. The unemployment rise is economy-wide; the report attributes it partly to agriculture and construction but gives no agriculture-only job figure.

resolvedSources.title: Updated Nationally Determined Contribution - Tunisia (English version)
resolvedSources.publisher: Republic of Tunisia, Ministry of Environment (submitted to UNFCCC)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Section 2.1.2 "Agricultural production", p. 28:

> Climate projections predict an increase in the frequency and intensity of droughts. These will affect cereal production, which would fall by almost 40% by 2050 according to the RCP8.5[17] scenario. The drop in yields that will affect olive production could reach 32%. The share of agricultural production in the national GDP would decrease by 5% to 10% in 2030, depending on the scenarios of economic openness of the agricultural sector. The impacts will be reflected in a drop in yields and a reduction in the area of tree and cereal crops, a loss of soil fertility and the area of arable land. The highest level of vulnerability is observed in central and southern Tunisia, and the level of vulnerability is particularly critical in the south (east and west).

Footnotes 14, 16 and 17, p. 28. Footnote 14 is attached to the water-resources paragraph (2.1.1), 16 to its vulnerable-groups sentence, and 17 to "RCP8.5" in the agriculture paragraph:

> 14 Scenario RCP 8.5 à l'horizon 2050.

> 17 Op. Cit 19.

> 16 Results published in the National Adaptation Plan Report (NAP-food security) - phase 2 - 2021-2021. Document being published by MARHP and AFD (Ministry of Agriculture, Hydraulic Resources and Fisheries - French Development Agency).

Adaptation section box, p. 55:

> This increase would vary according to the regions, in the best case (RCP 4.5) between 1 ° C and 1.8 ° C by 2050 and between 2 ° C and 3 ° C at the end of the century. In the most pessimistic case (RCP 8.5), the increase could reach 4.1°C to 5.2°C at the end of the century. Projections also show a decrease in precipitation (-10% to 30% in 2050), a rise in sea level (30 cm to 50 cm in 2050) and an increase in extreme weather events (floods and droughts).

Adaptation measures list, p. 65:

> Measure 8: Implementation of the updated National Drought Plan,
resolvedSources.notes:
Official English translation of the updated NDC (French original dated October 2021). Downloaded as PDF from the UNFCCC NDC registry. The cereal (-40% by 2050) and olive (-32%) figures trace to the MARHP/AFD National Adaptation Plan food-security study (SRC-TG-886). In that study's final tables, a cereal production loss of about 38-40% appears under RCP 8.5 at the 2100 horizon, not 2050 (see FND-TG-880). The precipitation range "-10% to 30% in 2050" does not match the -6% to -9% of the INM/PNA projections (SRC-TG-887) and has no stated source. The degree signs were split by the PDF conversion and are reproduced as converted.

**The olive figure matches the study.** The olive -32% equals the study's olive yield change under RCP 8.5 at 2050 (SRC-TG-886, Table 10). The sentence itself gives no horizon: footnote 17 ("Op. Cit 19") is the one attached to the agriculture paragraph, and footnote 14 ("RCP 8.5 à l'horizon 2050") belongs to the water paragraph.

**Local copy.** Downloaded on 2026-11-21 with a browser User-Agent to C:\Users\Taha\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\84d5bad6dc087fc3\6e966d88-81b3-402c-88d3-7630ed4be8fc\scratchpad\dl-drought-climate\ndc.pdf (12,815,022 bytes). The pdftotext output is ndc.txt in the same folder.

**Re-check on 2026-11-21.** Each extract was re-grepped in that text and confirmed verbatim, with page numbers taken from the page footers:
- p. 28: the agriculture paragraph (cereals "almost 40% by 2050", olive "32%", share of GDP "5% to 10% in 2030") and footnotes 14, 16 and 17;
- p. 55: the climate box;
- p. 65: Measure 8.

resolvedSources.title: Quatrième Communication Nationale de la Tunisie au titre de la Convention Cadre des Nations Unies sur les Changements Climatiques
resolvedSources.publisher: Republic of Tunisia, Ministry of Environment (submitted to UNFCCC)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Section 1.2.1 "Profil climatique", p. 19:

> Les observations des 40 dernières années (1978-2012) ont révélé ce qui suit :
> - Une augmentation importante des températures annuelles maximales, moyennes et minimales d'environ 2,1 °C, avec des différences régionales.
> - Une légère tendance haussière non significative des précipitations cumulatives.

English gloss: Observations over 1978-2012 show a large rise of about 2.1°C in annual maximum, mean and minimum temperatures, and a slight, non-significant upward trend in cumulative precipitation.

Section 5, p. 128 (history of projections):

> Dans la pratique, les premières projections climatiques concernant la Tunisie ont été réalisées dans le cadre de l'étude de la stratégie nationale d'adaptation du secteur agricole et des écosystèmes au changement climatique réalisée entre 2006 et 2007 par le Ministère de l'Agriculture, des Ressources Hydrauliques et de la Pêche avec l'appui de la GIZ. Ces projections climatiques aux horizons 2020 et 2050 ont été possibles grâce à des modèles et des scénarios dont le choix a reposé sur l'étude du Tyndall Center qui compare les résultats de quatre modèles SRES et le modèle HadCM3 avec ses scénarios moyens A2 et B2.

English gloss: The first climate projections for Tunisia were made in the 2006-2007 national strategy for adapting agriculture and ecosystems to climate change (agriculture ministry with GIZ), for 2020 and 2050, using HadCM3 under SRES A2 and B2.

p. 129-130 (INM 2015 study, SRES A1B), "Evolutions observées sur la période historique 1951-2010":

> Une hausse significative des températures durant la période 1951-2010 : un réchauffement moyen d'environ 2.1°C sur l'ensemble de la période 1951-2010 avec des différenciations selon les régions,

> Une baisse des précipitations comprise entre 2% à 16% sur l'ensemble du territoire par rapport à la période 1961-1990.

> Augmentation générale de la superficie touchée par la sècheresse en Tunisie, sous toutes ses formes,
> Augmentation générale de la fréquence des sècheresses extrêmes.

> La diminution des précipitations, à l'horizon 2050, varie entre 10% et 35% d'après la moyenne de l'ensemble des modèles. Elle peut atteindre 60 % sur certaines régions d'après quelques modèles, surtout dans le sud du pays,

English gloss: INM (2015) reports significant warming of about 2.1°C over 1951-2010 (the same 2.1°C that p. 19 attaches to 1978-2012), an observed precipitation decline of 2-16% relative to 1961-1990 over 1951-2010, a general increase in drought-affected area and in extreme-drought frequency, and a projected 2050 precipitation decline of 10-35% (ensemble mean; up to 60% in some regions and models).

p. 132-133 (MARHP/AFD 2021 downscaling, RCP 4.5 and 8.5, reference 1981-2010):

> Une augmentation de la température moyenne annuelle sur l'ensemble du territoire variant entre 1.6°C (RCP 4.5) et 1.9°C (RCP 8.5) à l'horizon 2050, soit une augmentation entre 8% et 10% par rapport à la période de référence 1981-2010.

> Les projections de la variation annuelle moyenne des précipitations montrent une réduction du volume global des précipitations moyennes sur l'ensemble du territoire tunisien à l'horizon 2050, variant entre (- 14 mm/an, RCP 8.5) et (- 22 mm/an, RCP 4.5), soit entre 6% et 9% par rapport à la période de référence (1981-2010).

p. 134-135, Table 26 (extremes, horizon 2050; consecutive dry days on p. 134, heatwave days on p. 135):

> Une augmentation du nombre de jours consécutifs secs (valeur moyenne sur le territoire) de l'ordre de + 9.3 jours/an à l'échéance 2050 [RCP 4.5] ... de l'ordre de + 17.1 jours/ an [RCP 8.5]
> Statistiquement non significative en 2050, cette tendance deviendra significative en 2100.

> Une augmentation du nombre de jours de canicules (valeur moyenne sur le territoire) de l'ordre de +31.9 jours en comparaison avec la période de référence [RCP 4.5] ... de l'ordre de +39.1 jours en comparaison avec la période de référence [RCP 8.5]
> Statistiquement non significative en 2050, cette tendance deviendra significative en 2100.

English gloss: Consecutive dry days rise by about 9.3 days/year (RCP 4.5) and 17.1 days/year (RCP 8.5) by 2050. Heatwave days rise by about 31.9 (RCP 4.5) and 39.1 (RCP 8.5) relative to 1981-2010. Neither is statistically significant in 2050; both become significant by 2100. (Table cells reassembled from a two-column layout; scenario labels in brackets added from the column headers.)

Section 5.2.2, p. 161-162:

> La possible migration vers le nord des étages bioclimatiques va induire une réduction des espaces favorables à l'agriculture, surtout pluviale, et une migration des espèces culturales vers le nord du pays.

> A l'horizon 2100, les aires favorables aux céréales (blés et orge) diminueraient en moyenne de 16% (entre -31% et +4% selon les modèles climatiques) pour le scénario RCP8.5 et en moyenne de -8% (entre -20% et +9%) pour le scénario RCP4.5.

> A l'horizon 2100, les aires favorables à l'oléiculture diminueraient en moyenne de 14% (entre - 27% et +7%, selon les modèles climatiques) pour le scénario RCP8.5, et en moyenne de -5% (entre -17% et +11%) pour le scénario RCP4.5.

p. 163:

> Il est ainsi attendu une perte de production en céréales de près de 40% à l'horizon 2050 selon le scénario RCP 8.5 et la baisse des rendements qui affectera les productions oléicoles pourrait atteindre 32%.

> La production céréalière sera gravement touchée, avec des réductions potentielles de 30 à 50 % de la contribution au PIB agricole d'ici 2100, équivalent à environ 4.669 MUSD, et des pertes d'emplois de 30% d'ici 2050.

p. 164:

> le changement climatique affectera la productivité des parcours naturels qui ne couvriront que 8 à 10% des besoins des cheptels d'ici 2050, comparé à un niveau de l'ordre de 16% en 2020.

(footnote 87 cites "Banque Mondiale 2023 : CCDR Tunisie - à paraitre".)

p. 164:

> La part de la production agricole dans le PIB national accuserait une diminution de 5% à 10% en 2030, selon les scénarios d'ouverture économique du secteur agricole

p. 165:

> En réalité on ne verra pas trop ces pertes, car les agriculteurs vont plutôt surexploiter les nappes et utiliser tout autre type d'eau pour subvenir à leurs besoins (y compris l'usage de l'eau potable et l'eau usée même sans traitement). En effet, l'expérience a montré (constat suite à la sècheresse des années 2016-2018) que les pertes de production pariassent faibles car les spéculations changent et certaines superficies des cultures augmentent. Aussi, le manque d'eau de surface est compensé par l'utilisation des eaux souterraines même quand la salinité est un peu élevée.

English gloss: In reality these (irrigated) losses will not be very visible, because farmers will instead overexploit aquifers and use any other water, including drinking water and untreated wastewater. Experience after the 2016-2018 drought showed that production losses appeared small because crop choices shift and some areas expand; the lack of surface water is offset by groundwater even when somewhat saline.

> l'impact économique négatif le plus important du changement climatique sur le secteur agricole est la perte potentielle d'emplois d'au moins 20% et une diminution du revenu des travailleurs de 30% à 50%

English gloss: The largest negative economic impact on agriculture is a potential job loss of at least 20% and a 30-50% drop in workers' incomes (footnote 95 points to the Adapt'Action PNA impacts study).
resolvedSources.notes:
292-page document dated December 2023, downloaded from UNFCCC and converted with pdftotext (Latin-1 re-encoded). Page numbers are the printed page numbers.

- **Internal contradiction on observed rainfall:** p. 19 reports a non-significant upward trend (1978-2012), while p. 130 reports INM's 2-16% decline relative to 1961-1990.
- **Swapped scenario labels:** On p. 133 the mm values are attached to the opposite scenarios from the INM portal (SRC-TG-887: RCP 4.5 = -14 mm / -6%, RCP 8.5 = -22 mm / -9%). The labels in this document are swapped: the source study itself (SRC-TG-886, p. 23) gives -14 mm for RCP 4.5 and -22 mm for RCP 8.5.
- **Horizon mismatch:** The "near 40% by 2050 under RCP 8.5" cereal figure does not match the source study's 2050 tables (SRC-TG-886).
- **USD conversion error:** "4.669 MUSD" equals 10% of the 2021 GDP the document itself gives (USD 46.69 billion, footnote 88), i.e. the whole agricultural GDP, not 30-50% of it. The figure is not used.
- **Local copy and verification:** Downloaded on 2026-11-21 with a browser User-Agent to C:\Users\Taha\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\84d5bad6dc087fc3\6e966d88-81b3-402c-88d3-7630ed4be8fc\scratchpad\dl-drought-climate\nc4.pdf (8,874,474 bytes, 292 pages); the Latin-1 text, re-encoded, is in nc48.txt in the same folder. On 2026-11-21 every extract above was re-grepped in that text. All are verbatim apart from line-break joins and the bracketed scenario labels. Printed page numbers were checked against the page footers:
  - p. 19: observed climate, 1978-2012.
  - p. 128: the 2006-2007 GIZ strategy.
  - p. 129: 2.1°C over 1951-2010.
  - p. 130: INM 2015 rainfall.
  - p. 133: -14 mm (RCP 8.5) and -22 mm (RCP 4.5), as printed.
  - p. 134: consecutive dry days.
  - p. 135: heatwave days.
  - p. 161-162: bioclimatic shift and suitable areas.
  - p. 163: cereals "près de 40% à l'horizon 2050", 30% job loss.
  - p. 164: rangelands 8-10%; share of GDP 5-10% by 2030.
  - p. 165: groundwater substitution after the 2016-2018 drought; "au moins 20%" jobs.
- **Unsourced job figures:** The two job-loss figures (30% for cereals citing the CCDR; at least 20% citing the PNA study) carry no method.

resolvedSources.title: Assessment of long-term trends and mapping of drought events in Tunisia
resolvedSources.publisher: Scientific African, vol. 21, e01766 (Elsevier); Mohamed, M.A.E.-H., Moursy, F.I., Darrag, M.H., El-Mahdy, M.E.-S. DOI 10.1016/j.sciaf.2023.e01766
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract:

> The analysis is based on monthly rainfall over 16 stations for a total period 62 years from 1958 to 2020 in Tunisia.

> The last ten years (2010–2020) counted as the warmest decade in the past 62 years.

> The results of MK test for annual rainfall data revealed decreasing the trend of annual rainfall had shown non-significant decrease at all stations except at seven stations (which has a non-significant trend increase). Annual mean minimum and maximum temperatures showed increasing trend with almost same rate (0.03 °C/year) and statistically significant at 1% significant level.
resolvedSources.notes: Only the abstract was read, through the DOAJ metadata API record for this open-access article. The full text on ScienceDirect (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2468227623002223) returned HTTP 403 when fetched on 2026-11-21 and was not opened. The finding uses only the abstract's headline results: no significant rainfall trend at any of 16 stations over 1958-2020, and significant warming of about 0.03°C/year. The series ends in 2020, so it does not cover 2021-2023.

resolvedSources.publisher: Institut National de la Statistique, Tunisie
resolvedSources.extracts:
National accounts table updated 3 August 2026. Indicator is annual percentage change in value added at previous-year prices. Table columns are calendar years 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.

> Agriculture, sylviculture et pêche | 0.2 | -2.0 | 2.1 | -16.1 | 8.6 | 11.7

English gloss: the sector including agriculture, forestry and fishing contracted by 16.1% in 2023 and grew by 8.6% in 2024. The page also contains current-price growth rates and sector shares; neither measures real annual growth.

relatedItems.title: Warming and drying are projected to cut Tunisian agricultural output and value added by roughly 15-33% by 2030-2050, but the circulating headline numbers trace back to two studies, and some are quoted at the wrong horizon or do not match the study they cite
Rainfed cereal output swings with rainfall and collapsed in the 2023 drought, cutting the harvest by roughly two-thirds or more
Tunisia imports roughly half of its cereals and almost all of its soft (bread) wheat, even in good harvest years
The state cereal system (Office des Céréales monopoly, decreed prices, CGC subsidies) built in 1962-1971 now strains public finances and blunts market signals
